children: Indian drugmakers are moving closer to launching affordable generic versions of Gilead Sciences’ long-acting HIV drug lenacapavir after a key regulatory panel recommended waiving local late-stage clinical trials, removing an important hurdle to bringing the landmark therapy to India.

Emcure Pharmaceuticals has already filed its injectable version with the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) and is hopeful of securing approval by the end of the fiscal, whole-time director and chief operating officer Samit Mehta said.
“We are very hopeful. It’s a high priority product for us,” Mehta told
in an interview, adding that the company is responding to regulatory queries on priority. “Typically, the DCGI has been fantastic with ARV drugs in terms of fast tracking approvals.”
Lenacapavir could be a game changer because its long-acting formulation sharply reduces the dosing burden.

Emcure, Dr Reddy's Laboratories and Hetero are among the Indian companies racing to develop generic lenacapavir under voluntary licences from Gilead Sciences. Gilead signed royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers in 2024 covering 120 countries, including India.

The race received a boost after the subject expert committee of the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) on August 11 recommended waiving local Phase III clinical trials and bioequivalence studies for generic lenacapavir, citing unmet medical need.
The recommendation covers applications from Dr Reddy's and Emcure, though final regulatory authorisation is still required. The panel has recommended post-marketing Phase IV studies in India.

The waiver is significant because it could cut development time and costs and allow Indian manufacturers to move more quickly toward commercialisation. Generic rollout across licensed low- and middle-income markets is expected from 2027, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said.

Mehta said a broad rule of thumb for commercialisation would be around 12 months from filing, though expedited regulatory reviews for antiretroviral medicines could shorten that timeline. Emcure is vertically integrated for the product, including its own active pharmaceutical ingredient, and has invested in manufacturing capacity for the tablets used alongside the injection.

“India’s CDSCO Subject Expert Committee’s recommendation to waive local Phase III clinical trial and bioequivalence study requirements for generic injectable lenacapavir is a significant step towards faster access to one of the most promising HIV prevention tools available today,” Carlota Baptista, MSF’s Global HIV HCV Access Advocacy Lead, said.
For India, the stakes are significant. An estimated 2.6 million people were living with HIV in 2025 and about 60,000 acquired HIV during the year, according to UNAIDS figures cited by MSF.

Price could be another breakthrough, Mehta said. Public indications from Dr Reddy’s and Hetero point to an annual treatment cost of around $40, covering the twice-yearly injections and accompanying tablets, though the final market price will depend on supply, capacity and competition. The generic price would be just a fraction of the drug cost in developed world where the price can exceed $28,000 to $42,000 annually.

Dr Reddy’s recently expanded its Gilead partnership to include the investigational once-yearly lenacapavir formulation. “If approved, investigational once-yearly lenacapavir may offer an additional long-acting HIV prevention option for people at risk of HIV acquisition, particularly in regions where access and adherence remain significant challenges,” Deepak Sapra, CEO, API and Services at Dr Reddy’s, said.

MSF, however, cautioned that the CDSCO panel did not recommend a similar Phase III waiver for lenacapavir's treatment indication in heavily treatment-experienced people with multidrug-resistant HIV, potentially leaving another important access gap.

title: Drugmakers move closer to launch landmark HIV drug as CDSCO eases approval process
